textbook:
Clean cutaway textbook illustration of ONE human TYPE I SKELETAL MUSCLE FIBRE (slow-twitch, oxidative), centered in a square 1:1 1080x1080 frame with generous negative space around the structures so labels can be attached later. The illustration's own neutral dark charcoal background must extend and touch all four edges of the canvas, filling it completely corner to corner. Do NOT draw any border line, rectangle outline, frame, mat, margin band, vignette or letterbox bar around the artwork, and do NOT draw the picture as a sheet or card lying on a surface.

HOUSE LOOK - match a refined educational plate exactly: a MUTED, slightly desaturated palette of soft dusty tints (never bright primary or cartoon colours), THIN clean outlines (never heavy black cartoon strokes), gentle soft shading with subtle dimensionality, and each structure its own distinct soft colour fill.

MORPHOLOGY: this is a single, long, perfectly UNBRANCHED cylindrical fibre, straight and uniform in width, lying diagonally across the frame and cropped by the picture's own square edge at BOTH ends — you must NOT draw a rounded end cap, a closed tip, or a circular/cut cross-section face at EITHER end; the tube is simply SLICED OFF by the frame boundary on both sides and must look like it continues invisibly beyond the picture, the way a photo of a length of rope crops the rope without showing its cut end. CRITICAL FRAMING CHECK: at BOTH ends, the fibre's own body colour must fully cover the picture right into the corner it exits through, touching BOTH edges that meet at that corner with no background-coloured triangle of empty space left over — imagine the square canvas was itself cut out of a much bigger picture of a long fibre, so the fibre's colour runs straight off two full edges (not just close to them) at each end. A flat cut face, a rounded tip, or ANY margin of background between the fibre and an edge at either end is a FAIL — verify mentally that the four corners are: fibre-colour, background, background, fibre-colour (diagonal composition) before finishing. Its own overall body colour is a deep, rich, muted red (myoglobin) - never pale or white. Do NOT taper, fork or branch it anywhere, and do NOT show it meeting another cell end-to-end.

NUCLEI (the single most important feature): draw ten to fifteen small, flattened, elongated, muted blue-violet nuclei distributed all along BOTH long edges of the fibre, each one lying immediately under the outer membrane, oriented lengthwise with the fibre. NONE may sit in the middle of the fibre's width - the entire central body must stay nucleus-free and open for the striated interior.

INTERIOR (revealed by a long cutaway window along the upper portion of the fibre):
- Parallel MYOFIBRILS running the length of the fibre, each banded with regular, precisely aligned cross-striations: a darker dusty-rose A band alternating with a paler cream I band, and a crisp, plain, thin slate-blue perpendicular line in the middle of every I band (structurally the sarcomere boundary — draw it as a bare line only, absolutely NO letter, number or tick-label drawn on or beside it), all in register across the fibre.
- Abundant amber-ochre MITOCHONDRIA with visible inner cristae, densely packed in a continuous rim just inside the membrane AND in long rows between the myofibrils - conspicuously abundant, not a token few, since their density is what marks this as an oxidative Type I fibre.
- A thin teal-blue SARCOLEMMA outlining the whole fibre.
- Two or three small, teardrop-shaped, pale SATELLITE CELLS tucked directly against the outside of the sarcolemma, distinct from and smaller than the peripheral nuclei inside the fibre.

EXTERIOR: alongside the fibre, running parallel to it in the surrounding space, draw a visible network of two or three slender CAPILLARIES (thin reddish tubes), close against the fibre to show its rich blood supply.

DO NOT draw: a short stubby cell that fits entirely inside the frame; ANY nucleus in the middle of the fibre's width; a branched cell or intercalated discs (that is cardiac muscle); a pale or white fibre with sparse mitochondria (that is a fast glycolytic fibre); an unstriated smooth tapered spindle; a cell wall, nucleoid, plasmids, flagella or cilia. Absolutely NO text, letters, numbers, labels, arrows, scale bars or watermarks anywhere in the image — this includes NOT writing a stray letter such as "Z" next to any structural line.
sem:
Photorealistic false-colour SCANNING ELECTRON MICROGRAPH of ONE human TYPE I SKELETAL MUSCLE FIBRE (slow-twitch, oxidative), centered in a square 1:1 1080x1080 frame with generous empty margin. Fill the whole square edge to edge with NO border, frame, vignette or letterbox bar, and do not render the image as a plate lying on a surface.

The specimen is a single, long, perfectly UNBRANCHED cylindrical fibre of uniform width, resting on a subtly textured flat substrate, running diagonally across the frame and cropped by the picture's own square edge at BOTH ends — you must NOT draw a rounded end cap, a closed tip, or a circular/cut cross-section face at EITHER end; the tube is simply SLICED OFF by the frame boundary on both sides and must look like it continues invisibly beyond the picture, the way a photo of a length of rope crops the rope without showing its cut end. Compose it ZOOMED IN and LARGE: the fibre's visible width should span roughly a third of the canvas, and its length must run corner to corner along the full diagonal of the square so both tips are pushed off-canvas by the framing itself — treat the picture edge as a hard crop through the middle of the fibre's length, not a boundary the fibre politely stops short of, and do NOT draw a blunt, torn, snapped, or otherwise visible end even close to the frame edge. CRITICAL FRAMING CHECK: at BOTH ends, the fibre's own body colour must fully cover the picture right into the corner it exits through, touching BOTH edges that meet at that corner with no background-coloured triangle of empty space left over — imagine the square canvas was itself cut out of a much bigger picture of a long fibre, so the fibre's colour runs straight off two full edges (not just close to them) at each end. A flat cut face, a rounded tip, or ANY margin of background between the fibre and an edge at either end is a FAIL — verify mentally that the four corners are: fibre-colour, background, background, fibre-colour (diagonal composition) before finishing. Do NOT taper, fork, branch it, or show it meeting a neighbouring cell end-to-end.

Render true 3D surface relief and nothing else: SEM shows only the outside, so draw NO internal organelles, NO visible sarcomeres, NO cutaway. What the surface does reveal: a fine, regular, ladder-like transverse rippling of the sarcolemma running the whole length (the surface signature of the sarcomeres beneath), and, most importantly, a row of small, discrete, gently raised OVAL BUMPS - each about the size of a grape relative to the fibre's width - running in a line along BOTH long edges (the flanks/rails) of the fibre where individual peripheral nuclei push up against the thin membrane from underneath. These are LOCALISED bumps on the edge rails only: the fibre's own overall diameter and its straight centreline must stay constant and perfectly cylindrical along its whole length - do NOT make the whole tube's girth pulse, swell or pinch in and out; only the thin edge rail shows the small nucleus bumps, one after another, like rivets along a seam. A fine mesh of slender capillary vessels lies alongside the fibre on the substrate. Crisp fine surface texture, shallow depth of field so the far end falls softly out of focus, cool studio microscopy lighting with a gentle rim light.

False-colour palette: a warm deep red to brick-red fibre surface (reflecting its dense myoglobin and mitochondria), the capillaries in a cooler pink-red, on a neutral pale grey substrate and a dark uncluttered charcoal background.

DO NOT render: a short capsule-like cell that fits entirely inside the frame; a smooth surface with no edge bulges (that would hide the peripheral nuclei); a branched or forked fibre; a pale/white surface (that is a fast glycolytic fibre); duplicated specimens; any floating debris. Single specimen only, clearly dominant in the frame. Absolutely NO text, letters, numbers, labels, arrows, scale bars, instrument data bars or watermarks anywhere in the image — this includes NOT writing a stray letter such as "Z" next to any structural line.
3d:
Semi-realistic 3D medical-illustration still of ONE human TYPE I SKELETAL MUSCLE FIBRE (slow-twitch, oxidative), centered in a square 1:1 1080x1080 frame with generous margin on a clean seamless dark studio background that fills the frame edge to edge. NO border, frame, mat, vignette or letterbox bar, and NOT rendered as a picture lying on a surface. Soft global illumination, gentle rim light, subtle subsurface scattering through the translucent sarcolemma, scientific-animation look.

MORPHOLOGY: a single, long, perfectly UNBRANCHED cylindrical fibre of uniform width, deep rich red in overall colour (myoglobin), lying diagonally across the frame and cropped by the picture's own square edge at BOTH ends — you must NOT draw a rounded end cap, a closed tip, or a circular/cut cross-section face at EITHER end; the tube is simply SLICED OFF by the frame boundary on both sides and must look like it continues invisibly beyond the picture, the way a photo of a length of rope crops the rope without showing its cut end. This is non-negotiable: imagine the camera is looking at a short SNIPPET cropped from the middle of a cable that is metres long — you must NEVER render a circular cross-section face, a rounded dome, or ANY kind of end-cap at either tip, and you must NEVER place nuclei, mitochondria or any other structure arranged in a ring/circle pattern at either end. Both ends simply run out of the picture. Compose it ZOOMED IN and LARGE: the fibre's visible width should span roughly a third of the canvas, and its length must run corner to corner along the full diagonal of the square so both tips are pushed off-canvas by the framing itself — treat the picture edge as a hard crop through the middle of the fibre's length, not a boundary the fibre politely stops short of. Do NOT taper, fork, branch it, or model it meeting another cell end-to-end.

NUCLEI (the single most important feature): model ten to fifteen small, flattened, elongated, softly glowing blue-violet nuclei distributed along BOTH long edges of the fibre, each lying immediately under the translucent outer membrane, oriented lengthwise. NONE may sit in the middle of the fibre's width.

A soft translucent cutaway along the upper portion reveals the interior in NATURAL, believable biological tones, clearly distinguishable, neither near-monochrome nor neon:
- parallel MYOFIBRILS with crisp regular cross-striations - deeper rose A bands alternating with pale cream I bands and a plain thin slate-blue perpendicular line in the centre of each I band, with the pale I-band surface immediately around that line left perfectly smooth and empty, showing only the fine longitudinal myofibril striping and nothing else, aligned in register along the fibre;
- densely packed, glowing amber-ochre MITOCHONDRIA, each with a few short straight parallel ridge-lines inside (plain fold-lines only — never a swirl, loop, scribble, or anything that could resemble handwriting or letters), filling a continuous rim just inside the membrane AND long rows between the myofibrils - conspicuously dense, since this density is what marks the fibre as oxidative Type I;
- two or three small pale SATELLITE CELLS modelled as flattened wedges pressed against the outside of the sarcolemma, distinct from the internal peripheral nuclei.

EXTERIOR: alongside the fibre, a network of two or three slender translucent red CAPILLARIES runs parallel to it in the surrounding space, close against the fibre.

DO NOT model: a short stubby cell that fits entirely inside the frame; ANY nucleus in the middle of the fibre's width; a branched fibre or intercalated discs (cardiac muscle); a pale/white fibre with sparse mitochondria (a fast glycolytic fibre); an unstriated smooth tapered spindle; a cell wall, nucleoid, plasmids, flagella or cilia. Absolutely NO text, letters, numbers, labels, arrows, scale bars or watermarks anywhere in the image — this includes NOT writing a stray letter such as "Z" next to any structural line.
